## Abstract

Ivermectin is a widely used antiparasitic drug with over 5.9 billion treatments distributed through global programs by 2025, yet its safety during early pregnancy remains uncertain. Early animal studies suggested teratogenicity at doses several-fold higher than the ones used in humans. Inadvertent exposures during mass drug administration campaigns have not shown clear increase in risk of harms. We aim to describe the effect of inadvertent ivermectin exposure during the periconception period on the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes.

The BOHEMIA trials were open-label, assessor-blinded, cluster-randomized, controlled studies conducted in Mozambique and Kenya to assess the effect of three monthly rounds of 400 mcg/kg of ivermectin mass drug administration versus 400 mg fixed dose of albendazole on malaria transmission. The first implementation took place between mid-March and mid-June 2022 in Mopeia (Mozambique) and the second implementation occurred between October 2023 and December 2023 in Kwale (Kenya). A nested observational prospective cohort sub-study was conducted alongside the main trial to evaluate the safety of drug exposure around the time of conception. This sub-study included women aged 13–49 years who became pregnant between two weeks before and the four weeks following exposure to either ivermectin or albendazole and were excluded from further treatment and monitored monthly until the end of pregnancy. The primary study outcome was incidence of pregnancy outcomes, considering a positive pregnancy outcome all live births without any detectable major congenital anomalies, and adverse pregnancy outcomes defined as a composite of miscarriages, stillbirths, and congenital anomalies. The trial was registered on clinicaltrials.gov (NCT04966702) and on the Pan African Clinical Trial Registry (PACTR202106695877303).

A total of 238 pregnant participants were enrolled in Mozambique and Kenya, 129/238 (54%) were potentially exposed to ivermectin and 109/238 (46%) to albendazole. Adverse pregnancy outcomes occurred in 24/105 (22.9%) women exposed to ivermectin and 15/77 (19.5%) women exposed to albendazole. Among the women with evaluable pregnancy outcomes, the odds of adverse pregnancy outcomes for ivermectin versus albendazole (OR = 1.22, 95% CI 0.59–2.50, p = 0.582) did not differ significantly between treatment arms.

Among women exposed to ivermectin or albendazole between two weeks pre-conception and the first four weeks of pregnancy, this study found broad confidence intervals do not exclude a clinically meaningful difference in either direction. It does however add meaningful data to a small cumulative evidence base on inadvertent ivermectin exposure in early pregnancy, even if the number of exposures documented to date remains too small to support policy or regulatory conclusions.

Unitaid.

Research in contextEvidence before this studyPregnant women are usually excluded from ivermectin treatment during mass drug administration campaigns. However, there has been little formal evaluation of the drug’s safety to date. We searched MEDLINE (via PubMed) and Google Scholar for articles published up to Aug 29, 2025, using the search terms “ivermectin” AND “safety” AND “pregnancy” AND “humans”. No language or time restrictions applied to this search. We identified one systematic review and meta-analysis that estimated the odds ratio for adverse pregnancy outcomes after ivermectin exposure during pregnancy, compared with unexposed pregnant women from comparable populations in controlled studies. It is unclear if exposure to ivermectin during pregnancy increases the risk of spontaneous abortions and stillbirths (four observational studies, 3042 participants: OR 1.15, 95% CI 0.75–1.78; very low certainty of evidence; one RCT, 832 participants: OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.18 to 2.14; very low certainty of evidence) or congenital anomalies (five observational studies, 3159 participants: OR 1.69, 95% CI 0.83–3.41; very low certainty of evidence; one RCT, 832 participants: OR 1.10, 95% CI 0.07 to 17.65; very low certainty of evidence). Taken together, those findings highlight a significant evidence gap concerning the impact of ivermectin use during pregnancy, this is particularly true about exposures during the first trimester as only 97 have been documented.Added value of this studyThis study adds information from the largest documented cohort of women exposed to ivermectin in the first trimester of pregnancy (particularly the first four weeks) to date. This study found no statistically significant differences between ivermectin and albendazole for any pregnancy outcomes. To our knowledge, this is the first study to provide insights into the safety of ivermectin among women who conceived after treatment or were inadvertently exposed during the earliest, undetectable stages of pregnancy.Implications of all the available evidenceThe findings from this study contribute further evidence on the safety of ivermectin in women who conceived shortly after drug administration or were treated during an undetected early pregnancy, complementing the cases described in the systematic review.

## Introduction

Ivermectin is a widely used systemic antiparasitic medication, with over 5.9 billion treatments distributed 1988 and 2024 through the Mectizan Donation Programme to combat onchocerciasis and, later, lymphatic filariasis.1 Its approved uses also include the treatment of strongyloidiasis and scabies. Additionally, ivermectin has potential applications in malaria control due to its endectocidal properties, which have been shown to reduce malaria transmission.2

Despite its widespread use, concerns remain regarding its safety during pregnancy. Initially, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) classified ivermectin as a category C drug, as early animal studies showed potential foetal risks, and there was insufficient safety evidence in humans. These concerns arose from early studies conducted in mice, rats, and rabbits by Merck during the 1990s.3 These studies showed teratogenicity at maternal-toxic doses ranging between 20 and 600-fold the usual doses in humans. However, subsequent studies revealed that the mouse strain (CF-1) used in initial maternal toxicity studies lacks P-glycoprotein (P-gp) expression in the placenta. This efflux pump plays a key protective role against ivermectin toxicity to the foetus.4 Therefore, evidence from these early animal studies need to be revisited.

Additionally, in ivermectin mass drug administration (MDA) campaigns for neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), women who are visibly pregnant and those self-reporting as pregnant are not offered treatment, but the remaining of women of reproductive age (WRA) are treated without formal pregnancy testing.5 This causes a high number of inadvertent exposures every year, which some have estimated to be 15–50% of women in their first trimester of pregnancy.6,7 Given the high pregnancy rates in endemic areas, some women were systematically left untreated year after year given successive pregnancies. This puts them in a particularly vulnerable position and greatly increases their risk of blindness. These factors, combined with the lack of evidence of harm despite large numbers of pregnant women exposed, and the discovery of the placenta P-gp in the 1990s,4,5 led the Mectizan program to leave treatment to pregnant women at risk of eyesight loss at the discretion of in-country program managers.5 However, the package insert was never modified.5

A systematic review conducted in 2020 included 893 documented ivermectin exposures during pregnancy in the context of MDA campaigns or clinical trials in Sub-Saharan Africa; of these, only 97 were reportedly exposed during the first trimester.8 It found no conclusive evidence linking ivermectin to adverse pregnancy outcomes, but due to limited sample sizes and study biases, the certainty of these findings remains very low.8 Given the continued demand for ivermectin in global health programs, a comprehensive evaluation of its safety profile during pregnancy is crucial for evidence-based policy decisions and improving public health outcomes.

The BOHEMIA clinical trials, recently conducted in Mozambique and Kenya, aimed at assessing the effect of ivermectin MDA on malaria transmission and randomized over fifty thousand individuals.2,9,10 Here we present the safety data of pregnancies potentially exposed to ivermectin.

## Methods

### Study design and participants

The BOHEMIA clinical trials were open-label, cluster-randomized, controlled studies. The studies were implemented in highly malaria-endemic districts in Mozambique and Kenya. The first implementation took place between mid-March and mid-June 2022 in Mopeia, a rural district in Zambezia Province, central Mozambique, and the second implementation occurred between October 2023 and December 2023 in Kwale, coastal Kenya.

The aim of the study was to assess the effect of three consecutive rounds of ivermectin MDA compared to a control group receiving albendazole on malaria transmission. Additionally, we explored how obstetric history and antenatal care services were associated with pregnancy outcomes.

Participants living in clusters assigned to receive ivermectin were given 400 mcg/kg of ivermectin (Stromectol®, from MSD, The Netherlands, supplied in 3 mg tablets in Mozambique and 3 mg tablets, donated by Edenbridge Pharmaceuticals in Kenya) once a month for three months. Participants in the control clusters received albendazole 400 mg fixed dose (generic chewable tablets from Cipla, India in Mozambique and G-Abzole® chewable tablets manufactured by Guilin Pharmaceuticals in Kenya) once a month for three months. Both treatments were administered under directly observed therapy to ensure adherence.

A nested observational prospective cohort sub-study was conducted alongside the main trial to evaluate the safety of drug exposure around the time of conception. This sub-study included WRA, defined as aged 13–49 years, who became pregnant either immediately before or in the four weeks following exposure to either ivermectin or albendazole. Pregnancy status was determined by conducting a urine pregnancy test (see procedures below).

### Randomisation and masking

Clusters were randomly assigned to receive either ivermectin or albendazole using computer-generated methods. The sponsor team and study statistician remained blinded to group assignments until the last study visit. However, for implementation purposes, the site teams were not masked to treatment allocation, and study participants were aware of the intervention they received.

### Procedures

Treatment was administered door to door, and intake was directly observed by fieldworkers residing in the clusters. At every study visit, a questionnaire was administered to all participants. All participants were required to meet the inclusion criteria and agreement to participate in the study by signing the informed consent/assent form for drug administration.

All WRA were provided with a pregnancy test to take in private prior to each treatment round, and were advised to avoid pregnancy throughout their participation in the study. Only those who tested negative were considered eligible for treatment. According to the manufacturer, the urine tests used (Healgen® One Step Urine Test, Geel Belgium for Mozambique and Wondfo One Step Urine Test, Guangzhou Wondfo Biotech Co., Ltd. for Kenya) could detect pregnancy as early as 6–15 days after conception.11, 12, 13, 14 As pre-specified in the protocol, women who self-reported being pregnant or had a positive pregnancy test at a subsequent visit one month after treatment intake were excluded from further treatment. They were then enrolled in a pregnancy follow-up cohort, and monitored monthly until the pregnancy outcome. Thus, the gestational age at exposure, which could theoretically span from weeks minus two to week four, was inferred from the timing of pregnancy tests alone, with no last-menstrual-period dating or ultrasound confirmation. Outcomes were ascertained based on the participant’s reports and their clinical records completed by attending clinicians at referral health facilities within the national health system.

Data were collected during monthly participants visits by a team of fieldworkers using digital forms programmed in Open Data Kit (ODK, https://opendatakit.org) platform in Android tablets. Data were uploaded regularly, depending on local internet connectivity.

### Outcomes and definitions

The primary outcome of the pregnancy follow-up cohort was the incidence of pregnancy outcomes in each country and overall. Live births without any detectable major congenital anomalies at the time of birth were classified as a positive pregnancy outcome. In contrast, adverse pregnancy outcomes were defined as a composite of miscarriage, stillbirth or congenital anomalies. Miscarriage referred to foetal loss occurring before 28 weeks of pregnancy (7 months); stillbirth to foetal death occurring at or after 28 weeks of pregnancy; and congenital anomalies, which were defined as major congenital anomalies identified at birth or shortly thereafter.15 Minor anomalies were not systematically ascertained and were not the focus of the study.

Additionally, we recorded cases of self-induced abortion, which referred to the voluntary termination of pregnancy, and cases of loss to follow-up, defined as participants who missed four consecutive follow-up visits or formally withdrew consent to participate in the study. These cases were excluded from the comparative analyses of live birth and adverse pregnancy outcomes. The evaluable pregnancy outcome population therefore included women with a known pregnancy outcome classified as either live birth without major congenital anomaly or adverse pregnancy outcome.

Beyond drug exposure, predictor covariates included baseline socio-demographic, socio-economic variables, as well as malaria prevention measures usage, all of which were defined using data collected at the enrolment visit for the analysis. Age was classified into three ranges: 13–17 years (adolescents), 18–34 years (young adults), and 35–49 years (mature adults). Given the studies were conducted in rural districts where close to 100% of the population live close to the poverty line, wealth index rank was categorized from Rank 1 (Least Poor) to Rank 5 (Poorest).16 The linear distance from every household to the nearest health facility was calculated based on GPS data using ArcGIS.17 Long-lasting insecticidal net (LLIN) usage was based on whether participants reported sleeping under a mosquito net the previous night.

Additional variables from the obstetric and antenatal history were collected and analysed as exploratory outcomes. Antenatal care indicators included the number of antenatal care visits, uptake of intermittent preventive treatment for malaria (IPTp), receipt of a LLIN, and reported intake of vitamins, folic acid and/or iron, and antiparasitic drugs during the antenatal care visits.

### Statistical analysis

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize participant baseline characteristics, stratified by treatment arm. Categorical variables were described using frequencies and percentages, and compared between groups using the chi-square test (or Fisher’s exact test when appropriate). Reported age was the only continuous variable analysed. Its distribution was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test and was considered approximately normal; therefore, group comparisons were performed using independent-samples t-tests. p-values were reported for all comparisons, with a threshold of p < 0.05 considered statistically significant.

Odds ratios (ORs) were estimated from logistic regression models. ORs were expressed as ivermectin versus albendazole, with albendazole as the reference group. For live birth, ORs greater than 1 indicate higher odds of live birth in the ivermectin group compared with the albendazole group, whereas ORs below 1 indicate lower odds of live birth in the ivermectin group. For adverse pregnancy outcomes, ORs greater than 1 indicate higher odds of adverse pregnancy outcome in the ivermectin group compared with the albendazole group, whereas ORs below 1 indicate lower odds of adverse pregnancy outcome in the ivermectin group. Because live birth is a favourable outcome whereas adverse pregnancy outcome is an unfavourable outcome, the clinical interpretation of the OR direction differs between the two outcomes.

Although adverse pregnancy outcomes were not rare in this cohort, ORs were used throughout to facilitate a direct comparison with our previous systematic review and metanalysis on the safety of ivermectin during pregnancy.18 All statistical analyses were performed using Stata 19 (Stata Corp., College Station, TX, USA).

### Ethical considerations

All adult participants signed informed consent. Consent was also sought from parents of minors and assent from adolescents aged 13–17 years. The study design, including pregnancy testing as among inclusion criteria was reviewed and approved by the WHO Vector Control Advisory Group. The protocol and informed consent/assent were reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Hospital Clinic of Barcelona (HCB/2019/113), the World Health Organization Research Ethics Review Committee (ERC.0003574), the National Committee for Health Bioethics of Mozambique (618/CNBS/21), KEMRI Scientific & Ethics Review Unit (4616), and Oxford Tropical Research Ethics Committee.18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23 Regulatory approval was obtained from the National Medicines Regulatory Authority of Mozambique (8309/380/DNF), the Pharmacy and Poisons Board of Kenya (ECCT/23/02/06), and the National Commission for Science Technology and Innovation of Kenya (NACOSTI/P/23/27319). The trials were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the Good Clinical Practice guidelines. The trial was registered on clinicaltrials.gov (NCT04966702) and on the Pan African Clinical Trial Registry (PACTR202106695877303).

### Role of the funding source

This work was funded and supported by Unitaid under the “BOHEMIA” grant. The funder had no role in study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation, writing of the report, or the decision to submit for publication.

## Discussion

In this open-label, cluster-randomized trial conducted in Mozambique and Kenya, exposure to ivermectin during the peri-conception period was not associated with a statistically significant increase in adverse pregnancy outcomes compared to albendazole. In endemic areas with high worm burden or prevalence, a single dose of albendazole or mebendazole is currently recommended by WHO for pregnant women outside the first trimester as preventive chemotherapy to control soil-transmitted helminth infections. Even though that the safety of these drugs in pregnancy has not been unequivocally established yet, the benefits are considered to outweigh the risks.19

These findings are aligned with those of a prior systematic review, which found no clear association between ivermectin exposure during pregnancy and adverse outcomes, though the certainty of evidence was low due to the small sample size (less than 900 women in total) and methodological limitations (only one randomized controlled trial).8 This study adds prospective data with structured follow-up. We observed no statistically significant increase in the risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, or congenital anomalies in the ivermectin group, in women exposed from two weeks before until four weeks after conception.

Not-surprisingly, antenatal care attendance and services received emerged as an important factor associated with pregnancy outcomes in our study in Mozambique, reinforcing global evidence on ensuring the health and wellbeing of both mother and child. Despite WHO’s recommendation of a minimum of eight contacts during pregnancy, antenatal care coverage remains suboptimal in sub-Saharan Africa,19,20 with only 58% attending at least four visits in 2023.21 In our study in Mozambique, this figure was even lower, with only 23.5% of women who had a live birth reporting four or more antenatal care visits, while 73.7% of those with adverse pregnancy outcomes had not attended a single antenatal care visit and this was consistently associated with the lack of key preventive interventions received in the antenatal care visits. This finding however should be interpreted carefully given that women experiencing very early miscarriages, by definition, do not attend antenatal care.

The current WHO recommendation, is that starting the second trimester, all pregnant women living in areas of moderate-to-high malaria transmission receive at least three doses of IPTp with sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine, iron and folic acid supplementation, deworming with albendazole and mebendazole, and the receipt of insecticide-treated mosquito nets,19,22 all of which were significantly more frequent among women with live births as opposed to adverse pregnancy outcomes in our study.

These findings highlight that improving antenatal care visits coverage and service uptake remains imperative to reduce the burden of adverse pregnancy outcomes and mitigate the risks associated with malaria in high-transmission settings.

As mentioned above, although mebendazole and albendazole are both classified as FDA pregnancy category C, the WHO recommends their use during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy for treating soil-transmitted helminth infections in highly endemic areas as their administration has been linked to improvements in maternal anaemia and neonatal outcomes.19 In contrast, ivermectin, despite sharing the same regulatory classification and being used in over 5.9 billion treatments worldwide, remains contraindicated during pregnancy.1 This precaution is largely based on early animal studies showing teratogenic effects at doses manyfold exceeding those used in humans. In this study, we observed no statistically significant differences in the occurrence of adverse pregnancy outcomes between the ivermectin and albendazole arms, among women with evaluable pregnancy outcomes. When expressed as ivermectin versus albendazole, the point estimate for adverse pregnancy outcome was above 1, but the confidence interval was wide and compatible with both lower and higher odds of adverse pregnancy outcome in the ivermectin group. Live birth and adverse pregnancy outcome were analysed using the same evaluable pregnancy outcome population and should be interpreted in opposite clinical directions, because live birth is a favourable outcome whereas adverse pregnancy outcome is an unfavourable outcome.

The study had three main limitations. Firstly, it relied on self-reported pregnancy outcomes, which might be subject to recall bias or inaccuracies, of note, no independent specialist review of congenital anomalies was undertaken. Secondly, the sample size was underpowered to detect relevant difference between treatment arms. Thirdly, although albendazole is recommended from the second trimester of pregnancy onwards, a study design comparing pregnancy outcomes with pregnant women who did not receive any treatment could provide more accurate data on ivermectin’s safety profile, although a recent meta-analysis on the use of albendazole during pregnancy found no increase in adverse birth outcomes, which provides some reassurance regarding the comparator.23 Additionally, all exposures occurred between two weeks pre-conception and the first four weeks of pregnancy, there is also some uncertainty around pregnancy dating due to the lack of ultrasound confirmation. Thus, inference about safety during the later first trimester, which includes the peak teratogenic period cannot be drawn from these data. Also, the proportion of women loss to follow up women was slightly higher in the albendazole arm, which may have had an untoward influence on the results. Finally, because adverse pregnancy outcomes were not rare, the magnitude of the ORs should be interpreted cautiously, as odds ratios may overstate relative risks. Despite these limitations this study contributes valuable data on the safety of ivermectin among women who became pregnant after drug intake or were treated while pregnancy was still undetectable pregnancy during the first days.

There are several options to better understand ivermectin’s safety profile across all stages of pregnancy. One would be additional reproductive toxicological studies in animal models, particularly primates; another one could be the creation of a database where inadvertent exposure during pregnancy in the context of individual treatment or MDA campaigns and the resulting pregnancy outcome are documented; finally, some conditions such as nodding syndrome have been associated with early-life exposure to high Onchocerca burdens, which could warrant the conduction of randomized controlled trials in pregnant women in endemic areas.18

In conclusion, this study found no statistically significant difference in the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes between pregnant women in the ivermectin arm and those who received albendazole. These findings add to the growing body of evidence around inadvertent exposure to ivermectin in pregnancy; however, the number of exposed pregnancies documented to date remains too small to draw policy or regulatory-level conclusions.
